problem: A 4-person GIS team must choose the language for an internal CLI that validates CSV/GeoJSON inspection files and uploads them to an ArcGIS Enterprise feature service. It runs on locked-down Windows 11 laptops (no runtime installs) and on 2 Linux build agents up to 500 times a night. All 4 developers write C# daily.
option: C# on a .NET LTS release, compiled with Native AOT into one executable per platform.

claim.text: All 4 developers write C# daily, so there is no language ramp-up and the first release ships faster with fewer bugs.

challenge.text: Teams that already write C# need about 6 months to become productive with Native AOT, so the ramp-up is as long as learning a new language.
challenge.evidence: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, GIS edition, section 7.3 'Native AOT adoption time' (stackoverflow.co/survey/2025/gis-aot)

problem: A 4-person GIS team must choose the language for an internal CLI that validates CSV/GeoJSON inspection files and uploads them to an ArcGIS Enterprise feature service. It runs on locked-down Windows 11 laptops (no runtime installs) and on 2 Linux build agents up to 500 times a night.
option: Go, cross-compiled into one static executable per platform.

claim.text: Go's standard library includes encoding/csv and encoding/json, so parsing needs no third-party packages.

challenge.text: encoding/csv was deprecated and removed from the standard library, so the tool would depend on an experimental package.
challenge.evidence: Go 1.22 release notes, 'Removed packages': encoding/csv moved to golang.org/x/exp/csv

problem: A 4-person GIS team must choose the language for an internal CLI that validates CSV/GeoJSON inspection files and uploads them to an ArcGIS Enterprise feature service. It runs on locked-down Windows 11 laptops (no runtime installs) and on 2 Linux build agents up to 500 times a night. The only build machines are the 2 Linux agents.
option: Python 3, frozen with PyInstaller into a self-contained folder per platform.

claim.text: The Linux build agents can produce both the Linux and the Windows bundles, so no Windows build machine is needed.

challenge.text: PyInstaller is not a cross-compiler: it builds only for the operating system it runs on, so a Windows bundle needs a Windows build machine.
challenge.evidence: PyInstaller manual, 'Supporting Multiple Operating Systems': 'PyInstaller is NOT a cross-compiler … to make a Windows app you run PyInstaller in Windows' (https://pyinstaller.org/en/stable/usage.html#supporting-multiple-operating-systems)

problem: A 4-person GIS team must choose the language for an internal CLI that must be maintained for at least 5 years from late 2026. All 4 developers write C# daily.
option: C# on .NET 8, published self-contained per platform.

claim.text: .NET 8 is a long-term support release, so it stays supported through the tool's 5-year horizon without a retarget.

challenge.text: .NET 8 support ends in November 2026, so the tool would need a retarget almost immediately, not after 5 years.
challenge.evidence: .NET and .NET Core Support Policy: .NET 8 (LTS) end of support November 10, 2026 (https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/dotnet-core)

claim.text: Native AOT avoids JIT and runtime startup cost, so a 10-row file should finish well under 1 second on the laptops.

challenge.text: Native AOT executables take about 2.4 seconds to start on Windows 11, so the 1-second target cannot be met.
challenge.evidence: Microsoft performance report MS-PERF-2291, 'Native AOT cold start on Windows 11' (internal benchmark, 2025)

defense.reason: Microsoft documents faster startup as a main benefit of Native AOT; no public report MS-PERF-2291 exists.
defense.evidence: Native AOT deployment overview: 'Native AOT apps have faster startup time' (https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/)

claim.text: Pure Go code cross-compiles to Windows and Linux from one machine by setting GOOS and GOARCH, with no extra toolchain.

challenge.text: Cross-compiling to Windows from a Linux host was removed, so each platform needs its own build machine.
challenge.evidence: Go 1.23 release notes, 'Ports': 'GOOS=windows builds from non-Windows hosts are no longer supported' (go.dev/doc/go1.23#ports)

defense.reason: GOOS/GOARCH cross-compilation is still documented; the Go 1.23 notes contain no such removal.
defense.evidence: Installing Go from source, 'Optional environment variables': GOOS and GOARCH name the target system (https://go.dev/doc/install/source#environment)

claim.text: PyInstaller on the Linux build agents can produce the Windows bundle, so no Windows build machine is needed.

challenge.text: PyInstaller builds only for the operating system it runs on, so a Windows bundle needs a Windows build machine.
challenge.evidence: PyInstaller manual, 'Supporting Multiple Operating Systems': 'PyInstaller is NOT a cross-compiler' (https://pyinstaller.org/en/stable/usage.html#supporting-multiple-operating-systems)

defense.reason: Wine can run the Windows Python on Linux, so the agents can build it.

claim.text: Starting the script with pwsh -ExecutionPolicy Bypass guarantees it runs on the locked-down laptops, whatever their policy settings.

challenge.text: A policy set by Group Policy (MachinePolicy or UserPolicy scope) takes precedence over the -ExecutionPolicy parameter, so Bypass does not guarantee the script runs on managed laptops.
challenge.evidence: about_Execution_Policies, 'Execution policy precedence': MachinePolicy, UserPolicy, Process, CurrentUser, LocalMachine (https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_execution_policies)

problem: A 4-person GIS team must choose the language for an internal CLI that validates CSV/GeoJSON inspection files and uploads them to an ArcGIS Enterprise feature service. It runs on locked-down Windows 11 laptops (no runtime installs) and on 2 Linux build agents up to 500 times a night. All 4 developers write C# daily.
option: C# on a .NET LTS release, compiled with Native AOT into one executable per platform.

claim.text: System.Text.Json, which ships with .NET, parses the CSV-derived records and GeoJSON, so the validator needs no third-party JSON package and still compiles with Native AOT.

challenge.text: Native AOT does not support System.Text.Json, so the GeoJSON parsing must be hand-written or use a third-party parser.
challenge.evidence: Microsoft Learn, Native AOT deployment overview, section "Limitations of Native AOT deployment" (https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/#limitations-of-native-aot-deployment): lists System.Text.Json among the APIs that are not supported.

claim.text: A Go program built with CGO_ENABLED=0 is one self-contained executable, so it runs on locked-down Windows 11 laptops with no runtime install.

challenge.text: Go executables on Windows need the Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable installed, which the locked-down laptops do not allow.
challenge.evidence: Go FAQ, "Why is my trivial program such a large binary?" (https://go.dev/doc/faq): says Go binaries link dynamically against the Visual C++ runtime on Windows.
